title: Corpus Christi
hook: the Eucharist carried through the streets

segments.voice: Yesterday, Trinity Sunday and the sign of the cross. Your line was one god, three persons.

In towns from Spain to the Philippines to Brooklyn, on one Sunday in early summer, traffic stops. Children in first-communion white scatter rose petals on the pavement. In some places the streets have been covered overnight in carpets of colored sawdust and flowers. A priest walks under a canopy carried on four poles, holding up a gold sunburst with a small white host at its center. Behind him, a brass band, a choir, families, the elderly with walkers. They stop at little altars set up on street corners.
screen: `TRAFFIC STOPS.` → `PETALS AND SAWDUST CARPETS.` → `A GOLD SUNBURST UNDER A CANOPY.`

segments.voice: Corpus Christi is Latin for the body of Christ. Catholics believe that at Mass the bread becomes Christ's body, truly present, and they already celebrate that every Holy Thursday. But Holy Thursday is crowded with the passion. So in the 1200s a nun in Belgium, Juliana of Liège, pressed for a feast of its own, with nothing else in the way. In 1264 Pope Urban IV established it for the whole Church, and tradition says he asked Thomas Aquinas to write the prayers and hymns. Some of the best known Latin hymns come from that work: Pange lingua, with its last verses, Tantum ergo, still sung at Benediction, and the long sequence Lauda Sion. The Gospel for the feast in one year is John six, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am the living bread which came down from heaven." The gold sunburst is called a monstrance, from the Latin monstrare, to show. The whole point is showing. The host isn't kept in the tabernacle today. It's carried out of the church, past the bakery and the bus stop and the bar, through the places people actually live. Christians understand the Eucharist in different ways: some see it mainly as a memorial, while Catholics, Orthodox and a number of other churches speak of a real presence. For Catholics, today's procession says something simple: the Christ they receive at the altar belongs on the street too. And this ends week ninety-six: Divine Mercy, the Good Shepherd, Fatima, the Ascension, Pentecost, the Trinity, and now the body carried through town.
screen: `CORPUS CHRISTI: THE BODY OF CHRIST.` · `JULIANA ASKS; URBAN IV, 1264.` · `A MONSTRANCE: FOR SHOWING.` · `OUT OF THE CHURCH, INTO THE STREET.` · then, large: `I AM THE LIVING BREAD WHICH CAME DOWN FROM HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: Walk slowly outside, even just to the corner and back, or picture your street from your window. Pass each door in your mind, the family with the new baby, the house that's been quiet since someone died, the shop owner, the person you've never met, and if you pray, pray for each one as you pass; if you don't, simply wish each household well.
Corpus Christi. Latin for the body of Christ: the feast of the Eucharist, established for the whole Church in 1264, kept with processions through the streets. Today's word.
Your line: carried through the streets. Petals on the pavement, and the traffic stopped. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: On Corpus Christi, the Thursday after Trinity Sunday or, in many countries, the following Sunday, Catholic parishes celebrate the Eucharist and often hold a procession carrying the host in a monstrance through the streets, stopping at outdoor altars for Benediction.

notes: Juliana of Liège (Mont-Cornillon) and Urban IV's bull Transiturus (1264); confirm.
Aquinas authorship of the Corpus Christi office is traditional and widely accepted, though debated; framed as 'tradition says'.
Gospel John 6:51–58 is Year A; Years B and C use Mark 14 and Luke 9. Script says 'in one year'.
Feast is Thursday after Trinity Sunday; transferred to Sunday in the US and many countries. In howItsDone.
